summary: Updates the SCTP specification in RFC 4960 with a way for a sender to ask for an immediate Selective Acknowledgment, using an Immediate bit in the DATA chunk header. Since unknown flags are ignored, it is compatible with older implementations. It was replaced by RFC 9260.

eli5.summary: A sender can tap a flag meaning please tell me right now that you got this, instead of waiting.

questions: immediate bit in sctp data chunk
how to avoid delayed acks in sctp
subtitle: A flag to ask for an immediate acknowledgment instead of waiting.

tldr.problem: When an SCTP sender needs an immediate acknowledgment from the receiver, it must wait for the receiver's delayed SACK timer, which can harm performance in situations like closing connections or filling windows.
tldr.mechanism: The I (Immediate) bit is added to the DATA chunk header. When set, it signals the receiver not to delay its SACK chunk.
tldr.outcome: The sender can now request immediate acknowledgments without changing the protocol's default behavior, and the extension is backward compatible because old implementations ignore unknown flags.

facts.label: Default behavior
facts.value: Backward compatible; ignored by old implementations

today: RFC 7053 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4960. It was replaced by RFC 9260, which consolidated all SCTP updates into a single specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: According to RFC 4960, SCTP receivers use delayed Selective Acknowledgments (SACKs). This delay is controlled by the receiver and is the default behavior. However, in some situations, delayed SACKs harm performance. For example, when an association is about to close, when the congestion or receiver window is full, or when applications like the SCTP socket API need to know immediately that data arrived, the sender cannot force an immediate SACK under the current protocol rules. This document adds a way for the sender to request an immediate SACK by setting a flag in the DATA chunk.
sections.eli5: When you send a message, the person who gets it might wait before saying they got it, to save time by confirming several messages together. Sometimes you really need them to say right away instead.

sections.title: The Immediate Bit in the DATA Chunk
sections.content: RFC 7053 adds the I (Immediate) bit to the flags field of the SCTP DATA chunk header. The DATA chunk format already had flags for E (end of message), B (beginning of message), and U (unordered); the I bit is position 0x08 in that flags byte. The bit appears in reserved space that RFC 4960 specifies should be set to zero and ignored on receipt. Since unknown flags are safely ignored by old implementations, this extension creates no backward compatibility problems.
sections.eli5: The header label on each message has a few flag bits. One new bit means please tell me right now when you get this.

sections.title: When and Why to Set the Immediate Bit
sections.content: The sender MAY set the I bit whenever it would benefit from an immediate SACK. The RFC gives examples: when the application requests it (such as when sending the last data before waiting for an SCTP_SENDER_DRY_EVENT), when the association is in SHUTDOWN-PENDING state, when sending a DATA chunk fills the congestion or receiver window, or when Stream Reconfiguration is waiting for all outstanding DATA chunks to be delivered. The receiver SHOULD NOT delay the SACK in response to the I bit; it SHOULD send the SACK immediately.
sections.eli5: The sender sets this flag in cases like finishing sending data and waiting for confirmation, or when filling the pipe completely and needing acknowledgment before sending more.

sections.title: Socket API Extension
sections.content: Applications using SCTP can request the I bit by passing the SCTP_SACK_IMMEDIATELY flag to socket functions like sctp_sendv(), sendmsg(), or the deprecated sctp_send() and sctp_sendmsg(). The flag is set in the snd_flags field of struct sctp_sndinfo or the sinfo_flags field of struct sctp_sndrcvinfo, depending on which function is used. This is purely informational in RFC 7053; actual socket implementations may extend their APIs in this way.
sections.eli5: A program can tell the SCTP system to set the flag when sending a message, using a special option in the send command.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content: A malicious sender could use the I bit to force a receiver to send an immediate SACK for every packet instead of bundling SACKs. This increases network traffic and processing cost. However, the additional packets would contain only simple SACK chunks (no gap reports or duplicate information), because gap reports only appear when packet loss or reordering is detected, and those conditions already trigger immediate SACKs. Thus, the extension does not introduce significant extra load. The feature is not negotiated; support is assumed based on configuration.
sections.eli5: A bad actor could spam the flag to force lots of tiny reply messages, but the system already sends replies quickly during packet problems, so the extra cost is small.
